title: Umm Habibah
hookLine: Abu Sufyan's daughter, who believed while her father opposed the Prophet, and emigrated to Abyssinia

cards: Her father would come to lead the Quraysh against the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. That father was Abu Sufyan, and his daughter Ramlah, known as Umm Habibah, had become a Muslim anyway.

She left Mecca with the emigrants across the sea to Abyssinia, far from her family. Years of opposition between her house and her faith. And then one day, in Ibn Ishaq's telling, her father walks into her room in Medina.

teach.b: Start in Abyssinia. Umm Habibah went there as an emigrant with her first husband, and her first marriage ended there, far from home.

Sunan Abi Dawud preserves what happened next: the marriage between her and the Prophet was arranged in Abyssinia, with the Negus, the Christian king who had sheltered the Muslims, giving the dowry on the Prophet's behalf.

The daughter of a leader of the opposition, married to him in a Christian king's land. Now the visit. Ibn Ishaq says Abu Sufyan came to Medina, still not a Muslim, trying to shore up a treaty his side had broken.
He went to his daughter's room and was about to sit on the Prophet's bedding. She folded it away. He asked whether she thought the bedding too good for him, or him too good for it.
She answered that it was the Messenger's place, and he was still a man who worshipped idols. Strong words to a father. The sirah keeps them as a picture of faith set above a family's pride.
But hold a second report beside it, this one in Bukhari. Years later, when news reached her of Abu Sufyan's death, Umm Habibah, on the third day, called for perfume and put it on.

teach.h: SHE MOURNS HER FATHER THREE DAYS.
teach.b: She said she had no need of perfume, but she had heard the Prophet say a believing woman should not mourn more than three days, except for a husband. She did mourn her father.
She just kept her mourning within what she had been taught.
Faith before family pride did not mean faith without family love. It meant knowing which came first.

how: Muslims honor Umm Habibah, Ramlah bint Abi Sufyan, among the mothers of the believers and among the emigrants to Abyssinia; her rule of mourning from Sahih al-Bukhari is part of how Muslims learn the limits of mourning.

o: Abu Sufyan's wife, who later accepted Islam
a woman of Abyssinia who sheltered the emigrants
Abu Sufyan's daughter, who believed despite him

p: her father, who opposed the Prophet
put on after three days of mourning

s: Umm Habibah was married to the Prophet in Medina
Abu Dawud says the marriage was arranged in Abyssinia, with the Negus giving the dowry.
she refused to mourn her father at all
Bukhari says she mourned three days, then put on perfume, following what the Prophet taught.
her father visited her in Medina before he became Muslim
Ibn Ishaq tells of the visit and the folded bedding.

games.q: your father, who still opposes the Prophet, comes into your room and is about to sit on the Prophet's bedding. what do you do?
o: let him sit; he's your father.
games.why: in Ibn Ishaq she folds it away and tells him it is the Messenger's place. Bukhari later shows her mourning him when he dies.

practice: Think of a place, if there is one, where what you hold most deeply and what your family expects don't line up, about faith or anything else you care about.
Breathe in and name what you won't let go of; breathe out and name one thing you love about that family member anyway. If you pray, pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Umm Habibah. Abu Sufyan's daughter, who believed while her father opposed the Prophet, married the Prophet in Abyssinia, and still mourned her father when he died. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'mother of Habibah', after her daughter; her own name was Ramlah.

carryVoice: Your line: faith before family pride. Faith first, and still never faith without love. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 2107 (the marriage in Abyssinia; the Negus gives the dowry)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Abu Sufyan in Medina; the folded bedding)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1280 (news of Abu Sufyan's death; perfume after three days)
